title: The treasure and the pearl (Matthew 13:44–46)
hookLine: a man finds treasure in a field and, in joy, sells everything to buy it

cards: A man is working a field that isn't his. Long day, hard ground. His tool hits something that isn't a rock.
He digs around it with his hands: a hoard, buried who knows how long ago, by who knows whom. He looks around. Nobody saw.
He covers it back up, walks home, and sells everything he owns. The house. The animals.
The good coat. The neighbors think he's lost his mind. He's grinning the whole time, because he knows what's in that field, and he buys it.

teach.h: ONE STUMBLES ON IT. ONE SEARCHES.
teach.b: Each story takes a verse or two in Matthew, and the two men arrive in opposite ways. The farmhand wasn't looking; he stumbled on it. The merchant was out seeking goodly pearls, as the King James puts it.

Christians hear both: some are found by faith on an ordinary afternoon, some search for years. Then the line the story turns on. Having found the treasure, the man "for joy thereof goeth and selleth all that he hath."

teach.h: FOR JOY, NOT BECAUSE HE WAS TOLD.
teach.b: Not because he was told to. Not a sacrifice he grits his teeth through. He's trading up, and he knows it.

teach.h: NOT A LOSS. A TRADE UP.
teach.b: Sell everything sounds like loss; the story hears a man who can't believe his luck. So what's the treasure? Jesus says the kingdom of heaven is like this.
One reading: God's kingdom, God's life, is worth more than everything you own, and finding it feels like joy.
Another turns it around: God is the one who gives everything to buy back the field, or the one "pearl of great price" is each person, and the one who sells all to have it is Christ.

teach.h: WHO IS THE BUYER? TWO READINGS.
teach.b: Both readings are still preached. One more detail.
Matthew's Greek word for treasure is thesauros: a store, a hoard, something laid up. Earlier in the same Gospel, Jesus says: "where your treasure is, there will your heart be also."
So the two stories ask one quiet question. What would make you that happy to let go?

how: Christians read these two parables as a picture of how much God's kingdom is worth, and some tell stories of people who left careers or comforts gladly to follow their faith. They're read in churches in the season when Matthew 13 comes around in the lectionary.

o: a debt owed to the owner of the field
a gift of money left at the temple
a hoard of riches stored up and kept

games.q: who's who in the two stories — tap the pairs.

s: the man sells everything as a painful sacrifice
the text says he sold it all "for joy thereof." he's trading up, and he knows it.
each of these parables takes only a verse or two in Matthew
Matthew 13:44 is the treasure, 13:45–46 the pearl. two tiny stories, side by side.
Christians all agree who the buyer is
one reading makes the buyer a person finding God's kingdom. another makes the buyer God, giving everything for us.

games.q: you're working someone else's field, and your tool hits a buried treasure. nobody saw. what do you do?
o: take it home tonight and say nothing.
cover it up, sell everything you own, and buy the field.
tell the owner and hope for a reward.
games.why: he hides it again and, "for joy thereof," sells all he has and buys the field. the story doesn't stop to judge his ethics. it's about the joy.

practice: Ask yourself what you'd give everything for, and let the answer come up on its own instead of reaching for the right one: a person, a way of living, a kind of peace.
If you pray, hold it before God and ask whether it's the treasure. Either way, notice how naming it feels: heavy, like duty, or light, like the man walking home from the field.

wordCard.voice: Thesauros. Greek for treasure, a hoard laid up: what the man found buried in the field.

orig.note: Greek: treasure, a store of valuables. the word in Matthew 13:44, and in 6:21: where your treasure is.

carryVoice: Your line: in joy, not duty. The man walking home from the field had it right; until tomorrow.
